instrument: BCA Board appointment, announced jointly with Telstra CEO Vicki Brady
position: Access to the governance of Australia's principal general business peak body, whose board carries the CEOs of Telstra, Commonwealth Bank, Wesfarmers, Google Australia and New Zealand and BHP Australia, and the chairman of Gilbert + Tobin. BCA President Geoff Culbert framed the appointment as strengthening the board's 'expertise in innovation and the digital economy'.
outcome: Sitting. AirTrunk joined the BCA in or around May 2025, six months before the NSW Data Centre Consultation Paper and eleven months before the NSW Data Centre Guidelines.
notes: The significance is structural rather than evidentiary. A board seat is not a lobbying record and no improper conduct is alleged or implied. What it establishes is that the operator most closely associated with Australia's largest data centre proposal holds governance-level access to the body that sets the cross-sector business policy agenda, at the same time as that body was submitting to a parliamentary inquiry into the sector and as its own members' projects were being assessed. The board is composed of serving chief executives of member companies, so this is the normal mechanism - which is precisely why it belongs in a database of influence rather than being left implicit.

recipient: NSW Legislative Council Public Accountability and Works Committee, Inquiry into Data Centres
position: Four recommendations: (1) 'Recognise data centres as a strategic economic opportunity for NSW and recalibrate policy settings, regulatory approaches and community narratives to enable and attract investment at scale'; (2) align the NSW approach with the Commonwealth Expectations to create a national and consistent approach so Australia can compete for investment; (3) give the new Investment Delivery Authority the ability to rapidly assess and recommend public infrastructure investments that support major private sector projects; (4) monitor planning reforms to ensure they deliver better performance, 'focusing on efficiency, consistency, and certainty in the planning system'. The submission states that 'the BCA has consistently called for a reduction in regulatory burden, and we do not support introducing additional regulation where it is unnecessary', and cites the BCA's own 2025 Regulation Rumble ranking NSW last for planning system performance as at June 2025.
outcome: The NSW Data Centre Guidelines of 17 August 2026 adopted the alignment-with-Commonwealth position (the Guidelines state they are 'consistent with the Australian Government's Expectations ... published in March 2026') and the IDA was already operating, with Round 1 endorsed on 27 March 2026 - five days before this submission was received. Recommendations 3 and 4 concern the IDA and planning performance, both of which remained live policy through 2026. No recommendation sought an environmental, emissions, water, noise, community-benefit, local-content or domestic-compute measure.
notes: ANALYSIS, clearly labelled. The submission's silences are as informative as its recommendations and were verified by keyword search after repairing the ff and ffi ligatures the text extractor drops. Against an inquiry whose terms of reference expressly cover (c)(ii) 'the role of on-site backup generation, including diesel and gas, and associated emissions and health impacts', (d) water usage and cooling, (e) local environmental and community impacts 'including noise, air quality and heat', and (g)(iii) 'the extent of public subsidies, concessions or state directed facilitation provided to the sector', the words that appear NOWHERE in 59,431 characters are: diesel, generator, back-up, NOx, nitrogen, noise, air quality, subsidy, payroll and land tax. It does address the subsidy question, in the negative and in one sentence: 'datacentre operators in Australia pay full taxes with no concessions'. It does address water, at length, with quantified figures. Recommendation 1 asks government to recalibrate 'community narratives', which is a request to change public discourse rather than to change an environmental standard - and the submission is explicit that the sector's problem is partly that 'the public debate can sometimes reduce them to symbols of trivial internet content'. The framing devices are two case studies: 'Amy's homework', a Year 10 student in Parramatta uploading a maths assignment, and 'Margaret's health monitor', a 78-year-old living alone with a heart condition whose wrist monitor alerts her doctor. Both are effective and both are true of some data centre traffic; neither bears on the marginal emissions, water or amenity impact of a new hyperscale campus, which is what the inquiry was asked about.

recipient: NSW Legislative Council Public Accountability and Works Committee
instrument: Public hearing, Jubilee Room, Parliament House - first witness
position: Under parliamentary privilege: data centre operators pay their way; the national electricity rules require all large load users including data centres to pay 100 per cent of connection costs and augmentations; operators will pay $10.3 billion in energy infrastructure to 2030 with $1.1 billion of that excess capacity available for public use; operators 'do not receive subsidies or tax incentives'; ABS water accounts show data centre water use is 0.04 per cent of Australia's and less than 1 per cent of Sydney's; and the widely repeated 25 per cent of Sydney's water by 2035 'is not based in fact' and 'was dismissed by IPART as being unverifiable, and it should be dismissed'. Also that data centres generate 'the highest gross value added per unit of energy of any industrial sector'.
outcome: Sydney Water's Managing Director Darren Cleary was asked on 22 May 2026 whether he stood by the 25 per cent forecast and answered 'We do, and we acknowledge the uncertainty'. The IPART characterisation remains unverified - research gap RG-042.
notes: DCA launched on 28 November 2025 and grew out of five operators; its members represent 86 per cent of national operational capacity. Note that DCA and the BCA - separately constituted, separately funded, with overlapping but not identical membership - made near-identical quantified claims to the same inquiry on the two questions most adverse to the sector: no subsidies, and low water use. Coordinated or not, the effect is that the committee heard the same two numbers from two independent-looking sources.

recipient: Public policy debate; cited by the BCA (Submission No 116), Data Centres Australia and the NSW Data Centre Guidelines
instrument: Oxford Economics, 'Surging Data Centre Connection Requests Drive Phantom Demand', 21 November 2025
position: That of roughly 44 GW of connection requests linked to data centre proposals received by AEMO in 2025, only about 6 GW of project capacity is expected to proceed and only 2.8 GW of actual electricity draw at maturity - '15 times lower than what is sometimes reported'.
outcome: Cited by the BCA to the NSW inquiry and, per the Chair's questioning on 22 May 2026, by Data Centres Australia as well. The NSW Data Centre Guidelines separately cite Oxford Economics work prepared for AEMO estimating that 6 in every 7 MW of connection requests are phantom. The two are consistent: 6 of 7 not proceeding is a 14 per cent conversion rate.
notes: CORRECTED 2026-10-22 (RG-078): this row named the BCA as the commissioner. The briefing's own page says 'This research briefing was commissioned by AWS. The analysis and findings are Oxford Economics.' AEMO separately commissioned Oxford Economics to forecast data centre electricity use; the Guidelines introduce the firm by that engagement and cite the AWS-commissioned briefing. The finding itself is that most requested capacity will never be drawn, which still stands as Oxford Economics' analysis.

position: That NSW ranked last of the Australian jurisdictions for planning system performance as at June 2025, performing well on transparency but lagging on efficiency, consistency and certainty for proponents.
outcome: Cited in Submission No 116 to support Recommendation 4. The ranking is the BCA's own publication, so it is a self-assessed benchmark offered to a parliamentary inquiry as evidence about the state's performance.
notes: Recorded because a peak body's own index, used as evidence in a submission about whether that state should regulate a sector less, is a conflict of method worth naming - not a conflict of interest in any legal sense, but the arbiter and the interested party are the same organisation.

A firm holding at least $234.4M in Australian government IT contracts - including to the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet, which now houses the Office of AI - is a member of, and co-chairs a programme of, a bilateral forum directed by a serving Commonwealth trade commissioner who previously led the opposition in the state where most of those contracts sit. This is entirely lawful and entirely normal in trade promotion. It belongs in the database because the Senate inquiry's terms of reference cover 'deals between Government and global AI companies', and because the Observatory's method is to map access rather than assume its absence.

recipient: Australian data centre policy debate (position, not advocacy)
position: By becoming a hyperscale data centre developer, TCS moved from being a supplier to government into the class of entity whose interests the NSW Data Centre Guidelines, the Commonwealth Expectations and the two parliamentary inquiries are actually about. TPG - its JV partner - is itself a BCA member. TPG's Jim Coulter frames data centers as an asset class at 'the intersection of green energy infrastructure, technology and real estate'.
outcome: Announced, subject to conditions precedent and statutory approvals. India-scoped: Chandrasekaran is quoted on building 'GW-scale AI data centers in India'. No Australian HyperVault facility is announced (RG-075).
notes: Recorded under channel 'other' because it is a market position rather than an act of advocacy, and because the lobbying table's enum has no value for 'became a regulated party'. The analytical point stands on its own: as at 18 September 2026 the BCA's membership includes at least one firm that is simultaneously a government IT contractor, a peak-body member, and a data centre developer. Whether HyperVault ever seeks Australian consent is the question that would convert this from a structural observation into a live conflict, and it is the highest-value forward-looking item in this layer.

person: Damian Parmenter CBE, former UK Ministry of Defence Director General AUKUS (2023 - 1 Feb 2025); Palantir Technologies UK Ltd 'Senior Counsellor' from July 2025
recipient: UK MoD and AUKUS trilateral networks (contacts 'especially in the US and Australia')
instrument: ACOBA business appointment advice letter, June 2025 (published c. Sep 2025)
position: Senior advisory role providing 'decision support' to the UK Head of Palantir on international defence and security issues, 'focused on international opportunities within Europe and the Indo-Pacific' (Parmenter's own description to ACOBA)
outcome: Appointment permitted subject to conditions: no use of privileged information; two-year bars on lobbying the UK government, on using in-office contacts to advantage Palantir (including 'in other governments and organisations'), and on advising on UK government/MoD bids; must not advise on the UK defence sector. Palantir confirmed adherence.
notes: ACOBA - a UK government ethics regulator - assessed the risk in writing: Parmenter 'would have amassed a network of contacts while in office especially in the US and Australia by virtue of his role at AUKUS ... a risk these contacts ... may be seen to offer new business development opportunities for Palantir'. As DG AUKUS he made no contractual or capability decisions (ACOBA), and Palantir attended his AUKUS outreach events; as DG Delivery and Strategy he visited Palantir 'to understand its work supporting Ukraine'. Australia has no published equivalent assessment for this or any Palantir appointment - the asymmetry is itself RG-090.
